analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicare-style health coverage to every U.S. resident, funded by a new income tax with national spending caps.
analysis.headline: Mediplan, a universal-coverage bill with 3 cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing in February 1994 and never reached a House vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a public health plan, Mediplan, covering every U.S. resident with the same benefits as Medicare, plus outpatient prescription drugs, well-child care, and extra coverage for pregnant women and low-income people. It would pay providers at Medicare rates with no extra billing to patients and cap the whole program's spending with a national health budget. It would be financed by a new income tax on individuals and health service providers, and private insurance would be limited to regulated supplemental policies. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed coverage, with the biggest gains for people who are uninsured or underinsured. Children under 23, pregnant women, and low-income individuals would pay no deductibles or coinsurance at all and get extra benefits like eyeglasses, hearing aids, and free preventive care [S3]. Most adults would face a $350 annual deductible (capped at $500 per family), a $2,500 individual out-of-pocket cap ($3,000 per family), and a new outpatient drug benefit with an $800 deductible and 20% coinsurance [S3]. Doctors and hospitals would be barred from billing patients beyond the approved rate [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially children and low-income people

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. resident automatically eligible for a public health plan with Medicare-level benefits, enrolled at birth with a Mediplan card [S2].

Adds outpatient prescription drugs to the Medicare benefit package, and gives children under 23, pregnant women, and low-income individuals free care plus extras like well-child visits, prenatal care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids [S2].
Caps out-of-pocket costs at $2,500 per person and $3,000 per family per year, and prohibits providers from balance-billing patients above the approved payment rate [S3].

Pays for it with a dedicated income tax on individuals and health service providers deposited into a Mediplan Trust Fund, and tries to control total costs with a national expenditure budget allocated by class of service [S2].

analysis.who_pays: A new income tax on individuals and on health service providers would fund the program [S2]. Health insurers would lose their core coverage business, since Mediplan would replace most private plans and insurers could sell only certified supplemental policies. Hospitals and doctors would be paid at Medicare rates, with payment rates adjusted to keep total spending within the national budget. Employers with group plans would have to keep extra benefits for current enrollees, enforceable through treble damages [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, health insurers, hospitals, and doctors

drawbacks.text: Most working-age adults would still owe a $350 annual deductible and would pay an $800 deductible plus 20% coinsurance on prescription drugs, so the plan is not free coverage [S3].
The bill finances universal coverage with a new income tax on individuals and health service providers, a real and visible cost increase for many households [S2].

A national Mediplan expenditure budget, allocated by class of service, would force the government to hold payment rates down to stay within the cap, which could squeeze hospital and physician revenues and strain access to care [S2].
Employers could keep richer benefits only for people already enrolled when the law passed, creating a two-tier system between current and new employees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine universal-coverage proposal with real protections: guaranteed eligibility, a drug benefit, an out-of-pocket cap, and no extra billing. The honest costs are the new tax and the hard limits on provider payment to hold total spending down, which is where any budget-capped universal plan generates pushback. The adult cost-sharing ($350 deductible, $800 drug deductible) was moderate compared with private insurance of the era, and children, pregnant women, and the poor would pay nothing. On balance it was a large, well-specified transfer of coverage to ordinary people paid for by broad taxation and reduced industry revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, got a single subcommittee hearing in February 1994, and died there when the Congress ended in January 1995, never reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the Mediplan Health Care Act on July 1, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees [S5].
Three additional Democratic sponsors, Reps. Coyne, Sabo, and Yates, were added in September 1993; no Republicans cosponsored [S3].
The bill was sent to the health subcommittees of both committees in July and August 1993 [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held on February 9, 1994, but no markup or committee vote ever followed, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health insurance industry, hospitals, and physician payment arrangements were better off, because Mediplan never advanced and the private system of the early 1990s remained intact. The tens of millions of Americans who were uninsured at the time gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo health system

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: House sponsor, Ways and Means Health Subcommittee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mediplan Act on July 1, 1993 and made introductory remarks on the House floor [S1].

for.name: 3 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors in September 1993 [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 1, 1993, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, held a hearing on February 9, 1994, and never reported it to the full House [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 1, 1993, sent it to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee, and never reported it [S5].

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Championed his own Health Security Act in 1993-94, which dominated the congressional health care agenda while alternative universal-coverage bills like Mediplan sat in committee.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a well-funded public advertising campaign against government-run universal coverage plans during the 1993-94 health care debate.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill's only recorded progress was a Democratic-controlled subcommittee hearing, and it never came to a floor vote.

industries.note: Mediplan would pay for core health benefits publicly, replacing most private coverage; insurers could sell only certified supplemental policies with loss-ratio floors of 70-80% and face criminal penalties for selling duplicative coverage [S2]. Their core revenue stream would largely disappear.

Providers would be paid at Medicare rates set to fit within a national spending budget, could not balance-bill patients, and would face a reduced fee for cesarean deliveries [S3]. Revenue certainty would come at the price of lower, budget-constrained rates.

The bill creates a new national outpatient drug benefit, adding millions of paying customers, but payment would follow a prospective methodology tied to a formulary and to overall budget caps, cutting pricing power [S2].

Mediplan would take over core coverage costs for employees, but any employer whose plan provided extra benefits would have to keep offering them to current enrollees, with a treble-damages private right of action for failures [S3].
HMOs would remain in the program as Medicare-style participating plans with regulated payment, keeping a managed-care role inside the public system [S3].
